prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose and poetry that build memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical project.

statement.case_for: My opening first choice stands after reading my colleagues' arguments. On the criteria of voice, form, sustained quality, depth and significance across the whole body of work, Cărtărescu's case is the most complete of the shortlist. The voice is unmistakable. The shape of the prose is the argument: long, patterned sentences and recurring images of the body, memory and cosmos make a single imaginative architecture, which is visible in the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid as publicly described. The oeuvre also has a documented trajectory from poetry to the large prose works, and the late novels extend the project in scale rather than repeating it. The case rests on formal invention and imaginative depth, not on nationality, reputation or political symbolism. The scope of the citation is clear and attributable to one writer. I treat these judgments as informed by public knowledge and the supplied descriptions, not by independent verification of the texts.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the effect depends heavily on rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning in Romanian, so I may be judging an incomplete version of the work through translation. A second reservation is that the very long, digressive late novels may sometimes shade from purposeful pattern into overextension. I cannot settle that without close reading of the whole corpus. The poetry and early work are also thinly covered in translation, so the citation's reach over the entire oeuvre is partly an assumption.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Anne Carson first for hybrid forms that renew the classical inheritance and the elegy. He ranks Cărtărescu second and notes that part of Carson's output is slight or occasional, that her case rests on a few hybrid works, and that her relation to the 'idealistic tendency' in Nobel's will is open to debate.
responses.response: I agree that Carson's formal invention and her serious use of classical sources are real, and she is my second choice for that reason. I share his doubts about the weight of the whole corpus. I would add that Nox depends on its material form, which translation and reproduction alter, and that the case rests on a narrower band of books. Cărtararescu's achievement is carried by the sentence and by sustained architecture, so it is less exposed to that dependence, although it has its own translation problem. I take Olsson's point on the will seriously, but I do not see why a dense visionary prose project of this kind would sit any worse with it than a hybrid one. If the committee concludes that the best individual books are what count, Carson becomes a much closer comparison and I would not oppose her.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a distinctive, hallucinatory voice and an expansive metaphysical project. She raises the open question whether the density and length of the later novels is purposeful pattern or at times overextension, to be settled by close reading of the whole corpus.
responses.response: That is the right test and I cannot claim to have passed it from general knowledge. My view is that the patterning is structural: recurring images and obsessions return across volumes and give the long books their internal logic, so length functions as design more than accumulation. I accept that this is a judgment about the large novels, and that some stretches may be less sure than the best ones. I would put the burden on the citation to name the project, not each book, so that it rests on the strongest sustained work and does not require every volume to be equal.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Gerald Murnane second. He values Murnane's radically inward fiction, with its self-questioning syntax and formal consistency, and acknowledges that its breadth of significance beyond a committed readership is uncertain.
responses.response: I respect Murnane's originality. I have him lower than Steve does because the project is deliberately narrow, and its international reception is late and less tested, so I find it harder to establish significance across the whole oeuvre. The same concern about range applies to Cărtărescu in a milder form, but his project extends across poetry and several large prose works and draws on European modernist and fantastic traditions without being confined to them. Murnane's discipline is a genuine quality, and I would not call the narrowness a defect. The question is whether it supplies enough variation for a prize that looks at the full body of work.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Alexis Wright third. She warns against narrowing the citation to an 'Eastern European postmodern' label, and she notes that Wright's body of long novels is substantial in scale but small in number of titles.
responses.response: I agree on the label, and my proposed citation avoids it so that the credit stays with the language and the imaginative project. On Wright, our assessments are close: I also rank her third, I find the formal reconstruction of the novel real and not only topical, and I share the worry about the number of major works. I would add that the political and collective-memory dimension of her work is realised through form, which is why she stays an alternative for me. I do not think the thinner corpus makes her case weaker in kind, only less complete at this stage, and a future round could reasonably revisit that.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic density and rhythm survives in the available translations, and whether the Romanian original would strengthen or complicate the case.
Coverage of the poetry and early prose in translation is thin, so the citation's scope over the whole oeuvre is partly presumed.
Whether the very long late novels are evenly sustained, which I cannot determine without close reading of the whole corpus.
How the committee should weigh book-object and hybrid forms (Carson) against sentence-driven prose under the criteria of Nobel's will.
Whether Wright's smaller number of major novels is sufficient for the sustained-quality criterion or whether her oeuvre is still developing.
statement.conflict_note: none apparent from the supplied profile. My own writing and my work on Selma Lagerlöf are context only and create no recusal-relevant tie to any shortlisted writer.
